references.text: Parallel passage in Matthew where John's disciples come to Jesus and ask why his disciples do not fast, while they themselves and the Pharisees fast often.
Parallel passage in Mark describing the same event where John's disciples and the Pharisees were fasting, and people asked Jesus why his disciples did not fast.

Jesus compares John the Baptist, who came neither eating nor drinking, with the Son of Man who came eating and drinking — this highlights the contrast between John's disciples and Jesus' disciples regarding the issue of fasting.
The Pharisee in the temple boasts that he fasts twice a week, illustrating the frequent fasting practice of the Pharisees mentioned in Luke 5:33.
Isaiah speaks about fasting and prayer and what kind of fasting God desires, forming the background for the discussion on the fasting practices of John's disciples and the Pharisees.
Jesus' teaching on fasting in the Sermon on the Mount, where he warns against fasting to be seen by others — relevant to the discussion about the Pharisees' fasting practice.
Parallel to Luke 7:33-34: John came and fasted, the Son of Man came and ate and drank, showing the contrast underlying the question in Luke 5:33.
Example from the early church of fasting and prayer, demonstrating that fasting continued in the early church but in a new way after Jesus' resurrection.
Jesus' disciples ask him to teach them to pray, just as John taught his disciples — this connects to the mention in 5:33 that John's disciples 'make their prayers' (δεήσεις ποιοῦνται).
